oewn-01777051-v.learner: to hold on to an idea, a thought, or a feeling.
examples: He had entertained hopes of being admitted to a sight of the young ladies, of whose beauty he had heard much.
Not one of you entertained a doubt, I suppose, of their being really married?

oewn-02497847-v.learner: to give someone something amusing to enjoy.
examples: He listened to her with perfect indifference, while she chose to entertain herself in this manner.

oewn-00713544-v.learner: to think about something and keep it in mind as a possibility.
examples: She would not even entertain the idea of selling the house.

oewn-00021667-r.learner: now and then, and not often.
examples: He spent the rest of the evening in walking about the room, speaking occasionally to one of his own party.
I think it is no sacrifice to join occasionally in evening engagements.

oewn-01824240-v.learner: to get pleasure out of something you are having or doing.
examples: Elizabeth, after slightly surveying it, went to a window to enjoy its prospect.
Her uncle and aunt, leaving her to enjoy them in quiet, set off by themselves.
I have now learnt to enjoy his conversation as an agreeable and sensible young man.
You had better return to your partner and enjoy her smiles.

oewn-01193481-v.learner: to take great pleasure in something.
examples: Mr. Bennet, in equal silence, was enjoying the scene.

oewn-01819595-v.learner: to give pleasure to someone, or to be pleasing to them.
examples: Sir William had been delighted with him.
You will have the honour of seeing Lady Catherine de Bourgh on the ensuing Sunday, and you will be delighted with her.

oewn-01193481-v.learner: to take great pleasure in something.
examples: She delights in long walks by the river.

oewn-01821281-v.learner: to please someone so much that they are held as if under a spell.
examples: The magician's tricks delighted the children, who could not look away for a moment.

oewn-06754000-n.learner: something you say to defend bad behaviour, or a promise you failed to keep.
examples: His pride does not offend me so much as pride often does, because there is an excuse for it.
She was then but fifteen, which must be her excuse.

connotation.why: casts the reason given as self-serving cover for a fault

oewn-06638953-n.learner: a short written note that says why someone was not there.
examples: He brought an excuse from his mother after missing two days of school.

oewn-05829462-n.learner: a very bad example of something.
examples: That leaking shed is a poor excuse for a house.

connotation.why: dismisses the thing as falling far short of what it claims to be

oewn-02191956-v.learner: to make a deep, ringing sound, like a big gun going off.
examples: The great bells dinned across the valley all morning.

oewn-00608245-v.learner: to fix something in a person's mind by saying it over and over.
examples: His father dinned the same warning into him every single night.

connotation.why: frames the teaching as wearing repetition forced on the learner

oewn-00827108-v.learner: to point something out to someone, or bring it to their notice, as a protest or complaint.
examples: She represented to her sister, as forcibly as possible, what she felt on the subject.
His wife represented to him how absolutely necessary such an attention would be.

oewn-00989377-v.learner: to describe or show something, usually as having some particular quality.
examples: Not as you represent it.
The letter represented him as a careless and ungrateful man.

oewn-02705339-v.learner: to take the place of something else, or to be equal to it.
examples: In the old money, one shilling represented twelve pence.

oewn-06524571-n.learner: a spoken or written request for help, for a job, or for a place at a school.
examples: The surprise of such an application was great indeed.
I must confess myself surprised by your application; I did not expect it from you.

oewn-00634572-n.learner: hard, steady effort put into a task.
examples: Mary had neither genius nor taste; and though vanity had given her application, it had given her likewise a pedantic air.
I never saw such capacity, and taste, and application, and elegance, as you describe, united.

oewn-00950950-n.learner: the act of bringing something to bear on a thing, using it for a particular purpose.
examples: The application of these rules to real cases is not always simple.

oewn-00818217-v.learner: to say that something is not true.
examples: Mr. Darcy, you cannot deny the fact.
When questioned by him, Denny denied knowing anything of their plan.

oewn-02217607-v.learner: to refuse to let someone have something.
examples: You excel so much in the dance, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me the happiness of seeing you.
The usual satisfaction of preaching patience to a sufferer is denied me.

oewn-02218972-v.learner: to turn down a request or a formal petition instead of granting it.
examples: The board denied his request for more time to pay.

oewn-10518284-n.learner: a person who is not named.
examples: He was as much awake to the novelty of attention in that quarter as Elizabeth herself could be.
There was no other way of accounting for such attentions from such a quarter.

oewn-13759620-n.learner: one of the four equal parts of something.
examples: Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner were half a quarter of a mile behind.

oewn-15259739-n.learner: a length of time of fifteen minutes, a fourth of an hour.
examples: He continued to apologize for about a quarter of an hour.
